column1: # Where each port actually is, in real degrees.
# Why this file exists. ports.tsv is a faithful transcription of the 1990
# reference table, and that table's coordinates are the old game's own sextant
# readings, not geography: it puts London at N65, Rio de Janeiro at S65 and
# Cape Town at S45. coast.tsv, by contrast, is real coastline. Rasterising one
# against the other left 21 of the 70 harbours with no land next to them, two
# of them in open ocean hundreds of miles from anywhere.
# So the two roles are split. ports.tsv stays the source of record for the
# things the source table is actually authoritative about, which is the trade
# data: which economy a port belongs to and what it is known for. This file is
# the source of record for where it sits. Nothing in ports.tsv changed, so the
# transcription can still be checked against the source line by line.
# A side effect worth stating plainly: this uses less of the reference than
# before, not more. The map is now ordinary geography, and the only thing kept
# from the table is the goods matrix, which is the part that is a table of
# facts rather than anyone's creative work.
# Coordinates are decimal degrees, north and east positive. They are ordinary
# geographic knowledge, not a dataset, so there is no licence to carry. The
# grid is 5 degrees a hex, so the bar is the right harbour on the right coast,
# not survey accuracy; a place named for an inland city is given its historic
# seaport and the note says which.
# scripts/gen_game_data.py asserts that every port lands on water, that no two
# share a hex, and that every one of them has land in an adjoining hex. A
# harbour with no shore fails the build.
